# Introduction

The dominating method for fitting regularized regression models is proximal
coordinate descent, which serves as the default optimization method in a range
of software packages, including glmnet\ [@friedman2010; @tay2023],
biglasso\ [@zeng2017], ncvreg\ [@breheny2011], skglm\ [@bertrand2022],
adelie\ [@yang2024], LIBLINEAR\ [@fan2008; @yuan2012], and
BlitzL1\ [@johnson2015]. These packages do not in fact run a single algorithm:
glmnet, biglasso, adelie, and ncvreg solve a sequence of weighted-least-squares
subproblems via inner CD (the IRLS-CD family); LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 do the same
with a proximal-Newton linearization\ [@lee2014]; skglm runs CD directly on the
original GLM loss with constant per-coordinate Lipschitz steps. Coordinate
descent has been investigated extensively, for instance with respect to
acceleration and parallelization, yet one aspect that has so far not been
investigated is the strategy of fitting the intercept.

In this paper, we are interested in the following optimization problem:
$$
\minimize_{\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R},\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p}
  \Big(
  P(\beta_0,\beta)
  = F(\beta_0, \beta) + G_{\lambda}(\beta)
  \Big)
$$ {#eq-primal-problem}
where $P$ is the primal objective, $F$ is the loss function, which attempts to
optimize the fit to the data, and $G$ is the penalty function that penalizes
solutions with large coefficients. $\beta_j$ is the $j$th coefficient and
$\beta_0$ is the intercept. Throughout the paper, we assume that $P$ is
separable and that $F$ is the per-observation-averaged loss
$$
F(\beta_0, \beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^\intercal \beta + \beta_0; y_i),
$$
where $f$ is a smooth, twice differentiable, and convex function. The averaging
keeps the global Lipschitz constant on the intercept, $L_0 = \sup f''$, free of
$n$, and aligns with the $(1/n)\cdot\text{loss} + \lambda\,\|\beta\|_1$
$\lambda$-scale used by the production solvers we compare against in
@sec-production-solvers. For brevity, we use the convention of denoting the
$i$th row and $j$th column of the design matrix $X$ as $x_i$ and $x_j$
respectively. Finally, we let $(\hat{\beta}\_0, \hat{\beta})$ denote a solution
to the problem in @eq-primal-problem. Although we will not generally assume that
$P$ is convex, we will focus on this case in our empirical work.

Intercepts are necessary when fitting regularized regression models, since the
results will otherwise depend on the locations (means) of both the response
vector, $y$, and the design matrix, $X$. Only under strong assumptions can the
intercept be omitted without leading to unwanted results.

Despite the importance of the intercept and the maturity of coordinate descent
as a method for fitting regularized regression models, the issue of how to
update the intercept has not been studied in the literature. This may also serve
to explain why existing CD implementations differ widely in their treatment of
it: glmnet (`type.logistic`) and biglasso (`alg.logistic`) expose a
user-selectable toggle between a local-Newton and an MM\ ($1/4$-Lipschitz) IRLS
surrogate, and this choice happens to also determine which intercept update is
realized---the local-Newton surrogate induces an exact 1-D Newton step on the
intercept, while the MM surrogate reduces to a constant-Lipschitz gradient step;
skglm 0.5 picks the gradient scheme implicitly through its constant-Lipschitz
design; adelie keeps the intercept implicit through a weighted-centered-features
parameterization of the inner Gaussian surrogate; LIBLINEAR leaves the intercept
unregularized inside the prox-Newton inner CD, whose QP-convergent sweep drives
it to its conditional minimum on the quadratic each outer iteration; BlitzL1
does the same and additionally runs a separate 1-D Newton convergence loop on
the intercept on the original loss after each subproblem. But as we show in this
paper, the choice of strategy can have a significant impact on convergence
speed, especially under response imbalance.

The three main strategies that we will consider in this paper are:

Gradient Strategy
:   The intercept is updated using a single gradient step before each pass over
    the coordinates.

Newton Strategy
:   The intercept is updated using a single Newton step, wrapped in an Armijo
    backtracking line search, before each pass over the coordinates. The line
    search accepts the full step ($\alpha = 1$) on the first attempt away from
    cold start and provides a safeguard in the cold-start or saturated-loss
    regime where an undamped step could overshoot.

Exact Strategy
:   The intercept is updated by solving the optimization problem in the
    intercept convergence before each pass over the coordinates, using either
    gradient or Newton steps.

For a first illustration, see @fig-first-example, which compares the three main
strategies on $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression on the w1a
dataset\ [@platt1998]. The Newton and exact strategies reach the optimal
solution at indistinguishable pass counts, and the gradient strategy is markedly
slower. The per-pass overhead of the exact strategy that we develop in
@sec-theory is not visible on a single panel; we isolate it in
@sec-per-pass-cost.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-first-example
#| fig-cap: Overall convergence for $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression on
#|   the real dataset w1a.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "first-example.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy)

layers = visual(Lines)

draw(
    layers * spec,
    axis = (; yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    figure = (; size = (500, 300))
)
```

@fig-first-example heralds the main message of this paper: the Newton strategy
is both reliable and efficient, the gradient strategy is too slow, and the exact
strategy pays a per-pass cost without a commensurate rate gain. The per-pass
cost verdict is established by @prp-exact-cost and quantified in
@sec-per-pass-cost. The Newton strategy's per-coordinate Armijo guard protects
against the narrow cold-start regime where an undamped step could overshoot.

The framework we develop is both diagnostic and explanatory: it predicts when a
solver's intercept update will slow under imbalance, and it explains why most
CD-based GLM solvers in current use have already made the right structural
choice within their algorithmic family. The strategy distinction sharpens to two
algorithmic regimes: direct CD on the original GLM loss, and MM-IRLS inner
solves that majorize $f''$ by a global constant. Within a local-weight IRLS or
prox-Newton inner solve the three strategies collapse onto the same exact update
on the inner quadratic (@sec-irls), so the framework's per-package bite is on
skglm 0.5---the only production direct-CD GLM solver in our survey---and on the
MM-style mode toggles of glmnet (`modified.Newton`) and biglasso (`MM`), exactly
the cases it flags as suboptimal.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Strategy Taxonomy
:   We introduce and formalize three intercept-update strategies---gradient,
    Newton, and convergence---that span the design space used by current CD
    solvers for regularized GLMs. The Newton strategy folds in an
    Armijo-backtracking safeguard that absorbs the cold-start regime where an
    undamped step could overshoot.

A Unifying Schur-Complement Analysis
:   We develop a single Schur-complement lens that parameterises each strategy
    by the cross-Hessian coupling $\rho_{0j}^2$ and the curvature ratio
    $H_{00}/L_0$. Short Taylor expansions and an envelope-theorem identity tie
    the gradient strategy's slow regime to the per-coordinate Lipschitz mismatch
    $H_{00} \ll L_0$, and a decomposition of the standard randomized-CD bound by
    coordinate yields the leading-order iteration-complexity ratio
    $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}} \sim L_0/H_{00}$ in the imbalance regime,
    which diverges as $\mu_0 \to 1$ for binary logistic regression.

Structural Classification of Production Solvers
:   We derive a classification of CD-based GLM solvers into four algorithmic
    families---direct CD, local-IRLS, MM-IRLS, and prox-Newton---and identify
    the intercept strategy realized by each. The classification correctly orders
    every package in our survey (glmnet, biglasso, skglm, adelie, LIBLINEAR,
    BlitzL1, ncvreg, Lasso.jl) and turns the configuration options in glmnet
    (`type.logistic`) and biglasso (`alg.logistic`) into a controlled empirical
    experiment.

Empirical Verification on Production Codebases
:   Five figures on the same imbalanced logistic problem confirm the framework's
    predictions: glmnet `modified.Newton` needs roughly five times more inner
    passes than `Newton` at tight tolerance (and the same gap survives on w1a, a
    real severely imbalanced LIBSVM problem); biglasso `MM` needs roughly ten
    times more than `Newton`; skglm 0.5 exhibits the predicted slow ramp;
    LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 both converge fast, as the framework predicts for
    prox-Newton solvers whose intercept reaches its conditional optimum each
    outer iteration; adelie matches the per-iteration cost of glmnet `Newton`,
    as the framework predicts for its centered-features local-IRLS realization.

Multinomial Extension
:   We extend the analysis to vector intercepts (multinomial logistic) and show
    that the rare-class regime turns the slowdown from a corner case into the
    common regime. Verified empirically on the Yeoh2002 pediatric ALL
    gene-expression panel (@fig-real-multinomial; $K = 6$ subtypes, rare classes
    at 6\% and 8\%), where the gradient strategy stalls along the rare-class
    intercept components while the Newton and exact strategies collapse onto a
    single trajectory.

## Related Work

The intercept-update question sits at the intersection of three literatures, of
which none has analyzed it as a separate problem. Intercept handling in CD-based
GLM solvers has been treated as a routine implementation choice across the
ecosystem of CD implementations. The original glmnet paper\ [@friedman2010] and
its all-GLM extension\ [@tay2023] expose two weight schemes for the logistic
IRLS inner solver---local weights and a global 1/4 upper bound, exposed via the
arguments `type.logistic = "Newton"` and `"modified.Newton"`, which the glmnet
documentation describes as a speed trade-off rather than as an
intercept-strategy choice. LIBLINEAR's newGLMNET solver [@fan2008; @yuan2012]
treats the intercept as the unregularized last coordinate of the prox-Newton
inner CD: each inner sweep takes a Newton step on the frozen quadratic, and the
inner CD's QP convergence carries the intercept to its conditional minimum on
the quadratic each outer iteration, without any separate intercept loop on the
original loss.^[Source:
<https://github.com/cjlin1/liblinear/blob/491c9f1/linear.cpp#L1972-L1977>.
`solve_l1r_lr` (`linear.cpp:1796`) appends the intercept as a constant feature
and skips it from regularization (`linear.cpp:1789-1790`); inside the inner CD
QP solve the intercept update is the pure Newton step `z = -G/H`
(`linear.cpp:1972-1977`), and the outer Newton loop closes without any separate
intercept loop on the original loss.] BlitzL1\ [@johnson2015] does the same
inside the prox-Newton inner CD, and additionally runs a capped 1-D Newton loop
on the intercept on the original loss after each subproblem, to gradient
tolerance.^[Source:
<https://github.com/tbjohns/BlitzL1/blob/aef8d02/src/solver.cpp#L27-L55>. The
loop is called from `run_prox_newton_iteration` (`solver.cpp:262`) after the
working-set CD pass and step-size backtracking.] celer\ [@massias2020] does not
support intercepts for $\ell_1$-logistic regression. So, the
*implementation*-side choice is thoroughly studied and varied in practice; the
*analysis*-side question---under what response distributions the choice
matters---has neither been asked nor answered.

A second thread is the partialling-out / Frisch--Waugh--Lovell tradition. For
linear regression the intercept can be sidestepped: centering the features zeros
the cross-Hessian $H_{0j}$ and yields $\hat\beta_0 = \bar y$ at the
unregularized optimum, leaving the slope subproblem decoupled from the
intercept\ [@lovell1963]. Glmnet leaves the intercept unpenalized on
translation-invariance grounds---penalizing $\beta_0$ would make the path depend
on the arbitrary location of $y$---and the FWL decoupling above is what makes
that choice essentially free along the Gaussian path: the intercept is recovered
as $\hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \bar x^\top \hat\beta$ after the slope solve. The
decoupling fails for non-Gaussian GLMs because the inverse link sits between
$\beta_0$ and $y$: the cross-Hessian acquires weights $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$
that no longer cancel under feature centering alone, and the closed form for
$\hat\beta_0$ vanishes. adelie\ [@yang2024] supplies the natural GLM analogue:
its proximal quasi-Newton method builds a weighted Gaussian surrogate at each
linearization and absorbs the intercept implicitly through that surrogate,
rather than as a separate CD coordinate.^[Source:
<https://github.com/JamesYang007/adelie/blob/d6a1229/adelie/src/include/adelie_core/solver/solver_gaussian_pin_naive.hpp>.
The inner Gaussian solver uses IRLS-weighted column means in its gradient update
(`solver_gaussian_pin_naive.hpp:87, 120`) and recovers the intercept at the end
of the inner solve as the weighted mean of the working response plus the
residual mean (`solver_gaussian_pin_naive.hpp:392`); the column means themselves
are built with the IRLS weights in the outer GLM solver
(`solver_glm_naive.hpp:366`).] The same argument explains why the framework of
@sec-theory has no bearing on Gaussian data: there the decoupling is already
complete, $L_0 = H_{00}$, and the gradient and Newton strategies coincide on the
intercept.

The third thread is majorization--minimization\ (MM). The constant $L_0 = 1/4$
that governs the gradient strategy in @prp-gradient-partial, and which skglm
uses as its global per-coordinate Lipschitz step (in its unaveraged form $n/4$),
is the binary specialization of the quadratic Hessian majorant used by
@bohning1992 to build an MM algorithm for multinomial logistic regression.
@hunter2004 give the canonical exposition of MM. @krishnapuram2005 apply
Böhning's bound to L1-penalized multinomial logistic regression, a direct
precedent for the multinomial extension of this paper. In regularized logistic
regression the same construction lives on as the `modified.Newton` mode of
glmnet and the `MM` mode of biglasso\ (@tbl-classification).
@prp-gradient-partial gives the quantitative cost: when the response is
imbalanced, $H_{00}/L_0$ shrinks to zero and the MM step loses progress in
proportion. The MM literature treats this as loose majorization; what this paper
adds is that for imbalanced logistic regression and rare-class multinomial
classification, it is the common regime, not a corner case (@sec-irls,
@fig-multinomial-sweep).

## Theory {#sec-theory}

In this work, we consider models where the loss function is the
per-observation-averaged GLM loss
$$
F(\beta_0, \beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^\intercal \beta + \beta_0; y_i),
$$
which includes the full family of generalized linear models (GLMs). We let
$\eta : \mathbb{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ be the function that maps the linear
predictor to the domain of the response variable. For GLMs, this corresponds to
the inverse link function. To simplify notation, we equivalently define $\eta\_i
= x_i^\intercal \beta + \beta\_0$ to be the linear predictor. In a GLM, the
response $y_i$ is modelled as a random variable from an exponential family, and
is assumed to depend conditionally on the linear predictor $\eta_i$ via $\E(y_i
\mid \eta\_i) = \ilink(\eta\_i)$, where $\ilink$ is the inverse link function.

To estimate the parameters of the model, $(\beta_0, \beta)$, we form a loss
function from the negative log-likelihood of the target distribution, modeling
its mean parameter through the inverse link function applied to the linear
predictor. A special property of the resulting loss function is that its partial
derivative with respect to $\eta$ is
$$
f'(\eta_i; y) = \ilink(\eta_i) - y_i = r_i,
$$
where we define $r_i$ to be the $i$th component of the *generalized residual*.
As a consequence, the gradient of the loss function with respect to $\beta_j$
can be expressed as
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0,\beta)
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial \eta_i} f(\eta_i; y_i)
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} r_i.
$$

We summarize the loss, link, and inverse link functions for the loss functions
we will consider in this paper in @tbl-glm.

  | Model       | $f(\eta; y)$                                                                                       | $\link(\mu)$                           | $\ilink(\eta)$                                       |
  | :---------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- |
  | Gaussian    | $\frac{1}{2}(y - \eta)^2$                                                                          | $\mu$                                  | $\eta$                                               |
  | Binomial    | $\log(1 + e^\eta) - \eta y$                                                                        | $\log\left(\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}\right)$ | $\frac{e^\eta}{1 + e^\eta}$                          |
  | Poisson     | $e^\eta - \eta y$                                                                                  | $\log(\mu)$                            | $e^\eta$                                             |
  | Multinomial | $\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\left( \log \left( 1 +  \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} e^{\eta_j}\right) - y_k \eta_k  \right)$ | $\log\left(\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}\right)$ | $\frac{\exp(\eta)}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} e^{\eta_j}}$ |

  : Loss functions, link functions, and inverse link functions for generalized
    linear models. Note that in the case of multinomial logistic regression, the
    input is vector-valued, and we allow $\log$ and $\exp$ to be overloaded to
    apply element-wise in these cases. {#tbl-glm}

### Coordinate Descent

Coordinate descent is an iterative optimization method that updates one
coordinate at a time, while keeping the other coordinates fixed. In the case of
the intercept, this means that we update $\beta_0$ while keeping $\beta$ fixed.
In other words, we take the derivative with respect to the $j$th coefficient.
Using the chain rule, this can be expressed as
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta)
  = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} f'(\eta_i; y_i).
$$

In our algorithm, we take a step in the negative gradient direction, updating a
coefficient or intercept by
$$
\beta_j^+ = \beta_j - \gamma_j \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta),
$$
where $\gamma_j$ is the step size. The step size can be chosen in different
ways, but the typical approach in a coordinate descent algorithms is to take a
Newton step. We first compute the second derivative with respect to $\beta_j$:
$$
H_{jj} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_j^2} F(\beta_0, \beta)
       = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}^2 f''(\eta_i; y_i).
$$

Letting $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$ be the *weights*, we can express the Hessian
diagonal element as
$$
H_{jj} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}^2 w_i.
$$

This leads to the following choice of step size:
$$
\gamma_j = H_{jj}^{-1}
        = \left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}^2 w_i \right)^{-1}.
$$

It may seem natural to also take a Newton step for the intercept, i.e. pick
$$
\gamma_0
= H_{00}^{-1}
= \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)^{-1}
= \left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f''(\eta_i; y_i) \right)^{-1}.
$$
But as we have already discussed, several state-of-the-art implementations of
coordinate descent for regularized regression take different approaches to
updating the intercept. The three main strategies that we have identified are
these:

1. A Newton step, setting $\gamma_0$ as above.
2. A gradient descent step, setting $\gamma_0$ to either the global Lipschitz
   constant with respect to $\beta_0$ or via a backtracking line search.
3. Solving the optimization problem of the intercept iteratively to convergence,
   using either Newton or gradient steps. In this paper, we will use Newton
   steps. And we will refer to this method as the *exact strategy*.

The coordinate descent algorithm, with the difference intercept update
strategies, is summarized in @algo-cd.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-cd
#| html-comment-delimiter: "//"
#| html-line-number: true
#| html-no-end: false
#| pdf-placement: "ht"
#| pdf-line-number: true

\begin{algorithm}
    \caption{Cyclic Coordinate Descent}
    \begin{algorithmic}
        \State \textbf{Input:} Data $(X, y)$, $\lambda > 0$, initial intercept and coefficients $(\beta_0, \beta)$
        \While{not converged}
            \For{$j$ in $\{1, 2, ..., p\}$}
                \State $\beta_j \gets \operatorname{prox}\left( \beta_j - \gamma_j \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)$
            \EndFor

            \If{intercept strategy is "Newton"}
                \State $\beta_0 \gets \beta_0 - \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$
            \ElsIf{intercept strategy is "Gradient"}
                \State $\beta_0 \gets \beta_0 - \frac{1}{L_0} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$
            \ElsIf{intercept strategy is "Exact"}
                \While{not converged}
                    \State $\beta_0 \gets \beta_0 - \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$
                \EndWhile
            \EndIf
        \EndWhile
        \State \textbf{Output:} $(\beta_0, \beta)$
    \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

The Newton branch of @algo-cd wraps the same Newton direction in an Armijo
backtracking line search, accepting the full step on the first attempt in the
common case and shrinking $\alpha$ only when the line search detects an
overshoot.

### What Sets the Intercept Apart

Before analyzing how the three strategies behave, it is worth stating plainly
why the intercept warrants a separate treatment from a regular coefficient. The
formal apparatus of the rest of @sec-theory turns on four facts that distinguish
$\beta_0$ from $\beta_j$:

1. **The intercept's design column is $\mathbf{1}_n$.** Treating $\beta_0$ as a
   coordinate is equivalent to augmenting $X$ with a constant column of ones.
   This single observation unifies several quantities that would otherwise look
   unrelated: $H_{00} = (1/n)\sum_i w_i$ is a mean of weights rather than a
   weighted mean of squared features; the global Lipschitz constant
   $L_0 = \|\mathbf{1}\|^2 f''_{\max}/n = f''_{\max}$ does not shrink with the
   data (for binary logistic this gives $L_0 = 1/4$); and the cross-Hessian
   $H_{0j} = (1/n)\sum_i w_i x_{ij}$ is the $w$-weighted column mean, so the
   intercept couples to *every* slope through a single scalar regardless of
   feature correlations.

2. **The intercept is unpenalized.** The regularizer $G_\lambda$ acts only on
   $\beta$, so $\beta_0$ is the only coordinate whose update is smooth---no
   proximal operator, no soft-thresholding, no non-differentiable optimality
   condition. This is what makes the various strategies in @algo-cd possible for
   updating $\beta_0$ in the first place.

3. **The intercept is never inactive.** Production-grade CD solvers prune slope
   coordinates aggressively via screening rules, strong rules, and working sets,
   so any particular $\beta_j$ is touched in only a fraction of passes and its
   average per-pass cost is correspondingly small. The intercept is in the
   active set of every pass by construction, so its per-pass treatment dominates
   the overall intercept-update cost in a way that no individual slope's
   treatment does.

4. **In IRLS-CD, the intercept update is a re-centering step.** Because its
   column is constant, the gradient $\partial_0 F = (1/n)\sum_i w_i r_i$ is the
   $w$-weighted residual mean, so a Newton step on $\beta_0$ zeros the
   weighted-mean residual of the current working response. The slopes never
   perform this role. This is the structural reason adelie can fold the
   intercept into a weighted-centered-features parameterization of the inner
   Gaussian surrogate, while it cannot do the same with an arbitrary slope.

Items 1 and 4 are why the gap $L_0/H_{00}$ that drives our main result is
unbounded under response imbalance: $L_0$ does not adapt to the curvature of the
loss at the current iterate, while $H_{00}$ collapses with $(1/n)\sum_i w_i$ as
the linear predictor saturates. Items 2 and 3 explain why the choice of strategy
is even available, and why its per-pass cost is not amortized away. The
remainder of @sec-theory makes these observations quantitative.

### Cross-Influence of Intercept and Coefficients

The Hessian of $F$ with respect to the intercept and the coefficients exposes
how the intercept couples to each coefficient. Letting $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$,
we have
$$
H_{jk} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_j \partial \beta_k} F(\beta_0, \beta)
       = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} x_{ik} w_i
$$
for the coefficient--coefficient block and
$$
H_{0j} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0 \partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta)
       = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} w_i
$$
for the cross-influence between the intercept and the $j$th coefficient. Two
qualitative observations follow. First, the coefficients couple to each other
*pairwise*, through the weighted covariance structure of the features:
correlated features produce large $|H_{jk}|$, which is the classical reason
coordinate descent struggles on such designs. Second, the intercept couples to
each coefficient *globally*, through the weighted mean of that feature, with no
dependence on correlations.

For the special case of squared loss, $w_i = 1$ and
$H_{0j} = (1/n)\sum_i x_{ij}$, so centering the features makes $H_{0j} = 0$ and
the intercept decouples from the coefficients entirely. For other losses the
weights depend on the linear predictor and the response, so $H_{0j}$ is a
$w_i$-weighted mean of $x_{ij}$, which is generally non-zero even after
centering.

#### A Normalized Measure of Intercept--Coefficient Coupling

To quantify how strongly the intercept and the $j$th coefficient are coupled,
the natural quantity is the normalized cross-curvature
$$
\rho_{0j} \;=\; \frac{H_{0j}}{\sqrt{H_{00} H_{jj}}} \;\in\; [-1, 1],
$$ {#eq-rho}
which is invariant to rescaling of the features and the loss function, and which
the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality bounds in $[-1,1]$. The two extremes are easy to
interpret: $\rho_{0j} = 0$ means the intercept and $\beta_j$ can be optimized
independently; $|\rho_{0j}| \to 1$ means a change in $\beta_0$ is fully absorbed
by an opposite change in $\beta_j$ (or vice versa), and the two coordinates are
degenerate up to that direction.

#### The Profiled Objective

The cleanest way to see why $\rho_{0j}$ controls the impact of the intercept
update strategy is to consider the *profiled* objective obtained by optimizing
the intercept out:
$$
\tilde F(\beta) \;=\; \min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta).
$$

The Hessian of $\tilde F$ is the Schur complement
$$
\tilde H_{jk} = H_{jk} - \frac{H_{0j} H_{0k}}{H_{00}},
$$ {#eq-schur}
and in particular
$$
\tilde H_{jj} = H_{jj} - \frac{H_{0j}^2}{H_{00}} = H_{jj}(1 - \rho_{0j}^2).
$$ {#eq-schur-diag}

@eq-schur-diag is the key relation. When $|\rho_{0j}|$ is close to $1$, the
profiled curvature $\tilde H_{jj}$ is much smaller than $H_{jj}$: most of the
diagonal curvature seen in $H$ is "borrowed" through the intercept and is
removed once the intercept is profiled out. Coordinate descent that re-optimizes
the intercept after every pass is effectively running on $\tilde F$, with
curvature $\tilde H_{jj}$; coordinate descent that leaves the intercept stale is
running on $F$, with the inflated curvature $H_{jj}$. The gap between these two
regimes is governed entirely by $\rho_{0j}^2$.

#### Strategies as Schur Approximations

This perspective lets us classify the three intercept update strategies by how
completely they remove the intercept--coefficient coupling. The key object is
the *gradient response* of the coefficient subproblem to an intercept step: if
we step $\beta_0 \mapsto \beta_0 - \alpha\,\partial_0 F$, the partial derivative
with respect to $\beta_j$ that the next coefficient update sees satisfies, to
first order in $\alpha$,
$$
\partial_j F(\beta_0 - \alpha\,\partial_0 F, \beta)
  \;=\;
  \partial_j F(\beta_0, \beta)
  - \alpha\, H_{j0}\, \partial_0 F(\beta_0, \beta).
$$ {#eq-gradient-response}
The Schur-corrected gradient $\partial_j F - (H_{j0}/H_{00})\,\partial_0 F$ is
the gradient of the profiled objective $\tilde F$ at the current $\beta$. The
three strategies differ in how closely the residual gradient in
@eq-gradient-response approximates that target.

We make this precise in three statements. The first is the substantive one and
is what justifies the profiled-objective viewpoint operationally.

::: {.theorem #thm-profile-equiv}
**(First-update profile equivalence.)** Let $F$ be twice continuously
differentiable and strictly convex in $\beta_0$ for every $\beta$, and let
$\tilde F(\beta) = \min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$. Suppose the convergence
strategy has driven $\beta_0$ to the conditional minimizer
$\beta_0^{(t)} = \arg\min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta^{(t)})$. Then the *first*
coefficient update of the next pass uses the gradient
$\partial_j F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = \partial_j \tilde F(\beta^{(t)})$,
and is therefore identical to a CD step on $\tilde F$ at $\beta^{(t)}$ with step
size $1/H_{jj}$. The step size satisfies $1/H_{jj} \leq 1/\tilde H_{jj}$ by
@eq-schur-diag, so it is a valid descent step size for $\tilde F$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By construction $\partial_0 F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = 0$. The envelope
theorem gives $\partial_j \tilde F(\beta^{(t)}) =
\partial_j F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)})$, which is the gradient used for
the first coefficient update of the next pass. The Hessian relation
$\tilde H_{jj} = H_{jj}(1 - \rho_{0j}^2) \leq H_{jj}$ yields the step-size
ordering.
:::

@thm-profile-equiv is the bridge between the Schur analysis and CD theory: *at
the start of each pass*, the exact strategy aligns with CD on $\tilde F$. The
catch is that this alignment lasts for exactly one coefficient update---by the
second update, $\beta_0^{(t)}$ is no longer the conditional minimizer, and the
equivalence breaks. The next proposition quantifies how quickly.

::: {.proposition #prp-exact-cost}
**(Within-pass intercept drift undoes the exact strategy's work.)** Starting
from $\beta_0^{(t)}$ with $\partial_0 F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = 0$, a
single coefficient update $\beta_j^{(t)} \mapsto \beta_j^{(t)} + \delta_j$
yields
$$
\partial_0 F\bigl(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)} + \delta_j e_j\bigr)
  \;=\;
  H_{0j}\,\delta_j + O(\delta_j^2).
$$ {#eq-intercept-drift}
Hence after a single coordinate update of pass $t+1$, the intercept gradient is
no longer zero, and the conditional-minimizer property that @thm-profile-equiv
depends on is lost.
:::

::: {.proof}
Taylor-expand $\partial_0 F$ in the $\beta_j$ direction around
$(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)})$ using $\partial_{0j} F = H_{0j}$ and
$\partial_0 F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = 0$.
:::

The practical reading of @prp-exact-cost is a *cost-versus-progress* verdict on
the exact strategy. Let $k_0$ denote the number of inner Newton steps consumed
at the end of a pass to drive $|\partial_0 F| < \varepsilon$. Because the
intercept subproblem $\beta_0 \mapsto F(\beta_0, \beta)$ is a smooth strongly
convex 1D problem ($\partial_{00} F = H_{00} > 0$ in a neighbourhood of its
minimizer), Newton on it converges quadratically and
$k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$---a small constant in practice. The empirical
decomposition in @fig-per-pass-cost confirms $k_0 \in [1, 6]$ across the
imbalance sweep. Each step costs $O(n)$ work. By the proposition, the
conditional-optimum status established by these $k_0$ steps survives exactly one
coefficient update of the next pass---by the second update it has drifted by
$H_{0j}\,\delta_j$. Outer progress is therefore upper-bounded by what one Newton
step on the intercept would have already delivered, since the first coefficient
update is the only one that benefits from the envelope alignment. The exact
strategy thus pays $k_0 - 1 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$ extra inner Newton
steps per pass with no commensurate per-pass rate improvement over the Newton
strategy. The overhead is bounded, not unbounded, but the verdict stands: every
pass pays for inner work that buys no faster outer convergence. The penalty
grows with the magnitude of intercept-coefficient coupling: when several
$|H_{0j}|$ are large, fitting the intercept tightly is wasted work because the
next coordinate sweep re-perturbs $\partial_0 F$ immediately.

The cost-versus-progress verdict above is sharpest in the cold-start, direct-CD
setting that drives this paper. Three regimes soften it. *Warm-started path
solves* along a $\lambda$ grid begin each subproblem with $|\partial_0 F|$
already small, so $k_0$ drops to one or two inner Newton steps and the $k_0 - 1$
penalty shrinks to zero---bare Newton and the exact strategy converge to each
other in this regime. *Strongly coupled designs*, where the envelope alignment
of @thm-profile-equiv buys a meaningful first-update gain, partially offset the
per-pass overhead, though the cyclic drift in @prp-exact-cost still applies. *At
the prox-Newton or IRLS linearization boundary*, the Hessian is recomputed for
the next subproblem and the within-pass drift critique no longer bites; we
return to this case in @sec-irls, where it underwrites the intercept handling in
LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1. The exact strategy is a defensible choice in these
regimes and the recommendation against it in the rest of this paper should be
read as scoped to the cold-start, direct-CD setting outside all three.

::: {.proposition #prp-newton-approx}
**(Newton strategy is a leading-order approximation.)** Suppose $f$ is
three-times continuously differentiable. A single Newton step on the intercept
satisfies
$$
\bigl|\beta_0^{\text{Newton}} - \beta_0^*(\beta)\bigr|
  \;=\;
  O\!\left(\frac{\sup_\xi |f'''(\xi)|}{H_{00}^3}\,
            \bigl(\partial_0 F\bigr)^2\right),
$$ {#eq-newton-error}
where $\beta_0^*(\beta) = \arg\min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$. For squared
loss, $f''' \equiv 0$ and the Newton step is exact.
:::

::: {.proof}
Standard one-step Newton error bound for the one-dimensional intercept
subproblem $\beta_0 \mapsto F(\beta_0, \beta)$ at the iterate $\beta_0$:
$|\beta^N - \beta^*| \le \tfrac{1}{2}|\partial_{000}F|/H_{00} \cdot (\beta -
\beta^*)^*)^2$. Bound $|\partial_{000}F| = |(1/n)\sum_i f'''(\eta_i)| \le
\sup|f'''|$ and substitute the linear-model estimate $|\beta - \beta^*| =
|\partial_0 F|/H_{00} + O(\cdot)$.
:::

@prp-newton-approx says that the Newton strategy matches the convergence
strategy at leading order, with an error that vanishes both as the iterates
approach the conditional optimum and as the third derivative shrinks. For
logistic regression $|f'''|$ is bounded by a small constant; for squared loss
the Newton step is exact and the two strategies coincide.

What we actually need to know is whether the Newton residual harms the *next*
coefficient update. The following proposition translates the one-step Newton
error into a perturbation of the coefficient gradient that the subsequent CD
pass sees.

::: {.proposition #prp-newton-coupling}
**(Newton residual perturbs the next coefficient gradient.)** Let $r_0 =
\beta_0^{\text{Newton}} - \beta_0^*(\beta)$ be the Newton residual, with
$|r_0|$ bounded as in @prp-newton-approx. The first coefficient update of
the next pass uses
$$
\partial_j F\bigl(\beta_0^{\text{Newton}}, \beta\bigr)
  \;=\;
  \partial_j \tilde F(\beta)
  \;+\; H_{j0}\, r_0
  \;+\; O(r_0^2),
$$ {#eq-newton-coupling}
i.e. the profiled gradient plus a bias of order $H_{j0} r_0$. The Newton
strategy is therefore as good as the exact strategy on a coordinate
$j$ whenever
$$
|H_{j0}| \cdot |r_0| \;\ll\; \bigl|\partial_j \tilde F(\beta)\bigr|.
$$ {#eq-newton-good-enough}
:::

::: {.proof}
Taylor-expand $\partial_j F$ in $\beta_0$ around the conditional minimizer
$\beta_0^*(\beta)$, using $\partial_j F(\beta_0^*, \beta) = \partial_j
\tilde F(\beta)$ and $\partial_{0j} F = H_{j0}$.
:::

The criterion in @eq-newton-good-enough has two regimes worth flagging.
*Asymptotically*, $|r_0| = O((\partial_0 F)^2)$ shrinks quadratically while
$|\partial_j \tilde F|$ shrinks linearly with the iterate's distance from the
optimum, so the bias becomes negligible. *Far from the optimum*, the inequality
can fail when $|f'''|/H_{00}^3$ is large and $|\partial_0 F|$ is large
simultaneously: this is the cold-start regime, particularly for losses where
$f'''$ grows with $\eta$ such as Poisson ($f''' = e^\eta$). In that regime the
linear model implicit in a single Newton step becomes a poor approximation, and
a safeguard, such as backtracking the Newton step until the loss decreases,
recovers the leading-order accuracy that @prp-newton-coupling promises.

The scope of @prp-newton-approx and @prp-newton-coupling is a single Newton step
at the current iterate: they pin down the per-step bias and coupling correction
that the Newton strategy delivers. How those per-step gains compound into
convergence across an outer solve is a complementary question, which §Results
answers empirically across the benchmark suite.

::: {.proposition #prp-gradient-partial}
**(Gradient strategy applies a fraction of the coupling correction.)** In
the local quadratic model of $F$ at $(\beta_0, \beta)$, the gradient
strategy with step size $\alpha = 1/L_0$ removes a fraction $H_{00}/L_0
\in (0, 1]$ of the coupling component $(H_{j0}/H_{00})\,\partial_0 F$ that
the Newton and exact strategies remove. Specifically, the residual
gradient after the intercept step is
$$
\partial_j F^{\text{grad}}
  \;=\;
  \partial_j F
  - \frac{H_{00}}{L_0}\,\frac{H_{j0}}{H_{00}}\,\partial_0 F,
$$ {#eq-grad-residual}
so the coupling residual is $(1 - H_{00}/L_0)$ of its pre-step value. In
particular, when $L_0 = \infty$, no coupling is removed.
:::

::: {.proof}
Substitute $\alpha = 1/L_0$ into @eq-gradient-response and rearrange.
:::

The qualitative reading of @prp-gradient-partial is that the gradient strategy
is fully effective only when $H_{00} \approx L_0$, that is, when the Lipschitz
bound is tight at the current iterate. Whenever $H_{00}$ is appreciably below
$L_0$---as happens for logistic regression once predictions become confident, or
whenever the weights $w_i$ are concentrated on a small subset of
observations---the gradient strategy leaves a residual coupling of order
$(1 - H_{00}/L_0)$ uncorrected, and coordinate descent continues to run on a
worse-conditioned objective than necessary.

The Poisson loss is the limiting case: $H_{00}$ has no global upper bound, so
$L_0 = \infty$ and $H_{00}/L_0 = 0$. By @prp-gradient-partial, the gradient
strategy applies no coupling correction at all and the coefficient subproblem
sees the full, uncorrected gradient. In this regime the strategy is not merely
slow but structurally inadequate.

#### Quantitative Rate Gap

The $H_{00}/L_0$ ratio also enters standard randomized-CD rate bounds, where it
controls how aggressively the gradient strategy can update the intercept.
Standard sublinear bounds for randomized proximal CD
[@wright2015; @nesterov2012; @richtarik2014] grow with a sum over coordinates of
a quantity of the form $L_j R_j^2$, where $L_j$ is the coordinate-wise Lipschitz
constant and $R_j$ the cold-start distance to the optimum along coordinate $j$.
The strategies enter this expression identically on coefficient coordinates but
differently on the intercept: the gradient strategy plugs in the global
$L_0 = \sup f''$, while the Newton and exact strategies use the iterate-level
$H_{00}$, which may be orders of magnitude smaller.

::: {.corollary #cor-rate-gap}
**(Rate gap, with a large-imbalance reduction.)** Let
$R_j^2 = (\beta_j^{(0)} - \beta_j^\star)^2$ denote the squared cold-start
distance to the optimum along coordinate $j$, with the intercept as coordinate
$0$. Decomposing the standard sublinear randomized-CD bound by coordinate yields
the upper-bound ratio
$$
\frac{T_{\mathrm{G}}(\varepsilon)}{T_{\mathrm{N}}(\varepsilon)}
  \;\lesssim\;
  \frac{L_0\,R_0^2
        + \sum_{j\ge 1} H_{jj}\bigl(1 - (H_{00}/L_0)\,\rho_{0j}^2\bigr)\,R_j^2}
       {H_{00}\,R_0^2
        + \sum_{j\ge 1} H_{jj}\bigl(1 - \rho_{0j}^2\bigr)\,R_j^2}.
$$ {#eq-rate-gap}
In the regime $|\beta_0^\star|/\|\beta^\star\| \to \infty$---for binary logistic
regression with cold start, $|\beta_0^\star| = |\mathrm{logit}(\mu_0)|$ diverges
as $\mu_0 \to 1$---the intercept term dominates both numerator and denominator,
and @eq-rate-gap collapses to
$$
\frac{T_{\mathrm{G}}(\varepsilon)}{T_{\mathrm{N}}(\varepsilon)}
  \;\sim\;
  \frac{L_0}{H_{00}(\hat\eta)}.
$$ {#eq-rate-gap-asymptotic}
For logistic regression, $L_0 = 1/4$ stays fixed while $H_{00}(\hat\eta) \to 0$
as imbalance grows, so the limit diverges. Outside that regime---in particular
at $\mu_0 = 1/2$, where $\beta_0^\star = 0$ kills the $R_0^2$ terms---the
asymptotic in @eq-rate-gap-asymptotic does not apply, and the full @eq-rate-gap
is needed.
:::

::: {.proof}
The standard sublinear bound for randomized proximal CD on a convex composite
$F = f + \psi$ with $f$ having coordinate-wise Lipschitz constants $L_j$ grows
with $\sum_j L_j R_j^2$. The Newton strategy's intercept update is exact at
leading order (@prp-newton-approx) and aligns with CD on the profiled objective
$\tilde F$ (@thm-profile-equiv), whose coefficient curvatures are
$\tilde H_{jj} = H_{jj}(1-\rho_{0j}^2)$ by @eq-schur-diag. The gradient strategy
uses the global Lipschitz $L_0$ on the intercept and, by @prp-gradient-partial,
removes only fraction $H_{00}/L_0$ of the coupling, leaving an effective
coefficient curvature $H_{jj}\bigl(1 - (H_{00}/L_0)\rho_{0j}^2\bigr)$.
Substituting these into the $L_j R_j^2$ sum gives @eq-rate-gap; retaining only
the $R_0^2$ term in the $|\beta_0^\star|/\|\beta^\star\| \to \infty$ limit gives
@eq-rate-gap-asymptotic.
:::

::: {.remark}
@eq-rate-gap is a ratio of upper bounds, not the iteration-complexity ratio
$T_{\mathrm{G}}(\varepsilon)/T_{\mathrm{N}}(\varepsilon)$ itself, and three
substitutions inside that derivation are sharp only under further structure: the
strategies fix the intercept-update schedule rather than sampling it uniformly
with the coefficient draws; $H_{00}$ is an iterate-level Hessian entry, not the
fixed coordinate Lipschitz constant the CD bound ingests; and the Schur
reduction is exact at iterates where the intercept has reached its conditional
minimum and only approximate after a single Newton step. What survives is the
scaling: as the intercept channel degrades ($H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$) the upper-bound
ratio diverges, and @fig-rate-gap confirms the empirical ratio follows the same
scaling.
:::

Two regimes inside @eq-rate-gap are worth flagging. **Strongly coupled designs**
($\bar\rho^2 \to 1$, e.g. uncentered designs where the intercept absorbs the
column means): the denominator's Schur term collapses and the ratio gains an
additional factor of order $1/(1-\bar\rho^2)$. **Standardized designs**
($\rho_{0j} \approx 0$): the Schur correction is inactive, but
@eq-rate-gap-asymptotic still diverges via the intercept's $R_0^2$ dominance.
The two channels---per-coordinate Lipschitz mismatch on the intercept, and Schur
coupling propagated to the coefficients---are independent, and both ride on the
same $H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$ regime.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-rate-gap
#| fig-cap: Empirical $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$ (pass count to relative
#|   gap $10^{-6}$) versus the full bound-ratio @eq-rate-gap evaluated at the
#|   Newton-converged iterate ($R_j^2 = (\beta_j^\star)^2$ on the standardized
#|   design, with $H_{00}$, $H_{jj}$, and $\rho_{0j}^2$ taken at the same
#|   iterate), swept over response imbalance $\mu_0$ on the standardized
#|   logistic problem of @fig-mu-extreme ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$,
#|   $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$). The two curves track across the full
#|   $\mu_0$ range; the large-imbalance reduction $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$ of
#|   @eq-rate-gap-asymptotic is the limit reached only as $\mu_0 \to 1$, when
#|   $|\beta_0^\star| \gg \|\beta^\star\|$.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "rate-gap.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["records"])
df_long = stack(
    df,
    [:empirical_ratio, :full_ratio];
    variable_name = :quantity,
    value_name = :ratio,
)
df_long.quantity = map(df_long.quantity) do q
    q == "empirical_ratio" ? "Empirical T_G / T_N" :
    "Predicted (eq-rate-gap)"
end

spec = data(df_long) * mapping(:μ0, :ratio, color = :quantity)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Response imbalance μ₀",
        ylabel = "T_G / T_N",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

@fig-rate-gap shows the full bound ratio @eq-rate-gap tracking empirical
$T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$ across the full $\mu_0$ range. At $\mu_0 = 0.5$
the intercept's $R_0^2$ term vanishes and @eq-rate-gap reduces to a
slope-weighted ratio close to one---matching the empirical pass-count parity
there, which the large-imbalance limit $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$ of
@eq-rate-gap-asymptotic would have over-predicted by a factor of $\sim 3$. The
empirical ratio sits a roughly constant factor below the predicted curve at
every $\mu_0$; that residual is the upper-bound slack of the CD inequality
itself (see the remark following @eq-rate-gap). As $\mu_0 \to 1$, the intercept
term dominates and the predicted curve approaches $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$,
recovering @eq-rate-gap-asymptotic.

@fig-rate-gap sweeps $\mu_0$ and so probes the $H_{00}/L_0$ axis of the framing
while keeping the second axis $\bar\rho^2$ close to zero (the design is
standardized). The complementary slice---holding $\mu_0$ fixed and toggling
feature centering---isolates $\bar\rho^2$ directly. On the same problem family
with `means = :random` (so each column has an $O(1)$ mean), running on the raw
matrix gives weighted $\bar\rho^2 \approx 0.5$ where standardizing drives it
below $5\times 10^{-3}$. @fig-rho-centering shows the resulting jump in
$T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$ at $\mu_0 \in \{0.5,\, 0.9\}$: centering matters
in both regimes, the leading-order ratio
$(1 - (H_{00}/L_0)\bar\rho^2)/(1 - \bar\rho^2)$ captures the direction, and the
empirical jump sits a constant factor above the prediction---the same
upper-bound slack visible in @fig-rate-gap. The Schur framing's second axis is
therefore visible empirically, not just absorbed into the asymptotic limit of
@cor-rate-gap.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-rho-centering
#| fig-cap: Isolating the $\bar\rho^2$ axis. Holding $\mu_0$ fixed and toggling
#|   feature centering moves $\bar\rho^2$ from $\approx 0$ (standardized) to
#|   $\approx 0.5$ (uncentered, with $O(1)$ per-column means) while leaving
#|   $H_{00}/L_0$ approximately fixed. Empirical $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$
#|   at relative-gap tolerance $10^{-6}$ tracks the eq-rate-gap leading-order
#|   prediction $(1 - (H_{00}/L_0)\bar\rho^2)/(1 - \bar\rho^2)$ along this
#|   second axis, with the same constant-factor upper-bound slack @fig-rate-gap
#|   exhibits, on a problem with $n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, and $\lambda =
#|   0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "rho-centering.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["records"])

df_long = stack(
    df,
    [:empirical_ratio, :predicted_ratio];
    variable_name = :quantity,
    value_name = :ratio,
)
df_long.quantity = map(df_long.quantity) do q
    q == "empirical_ratio" ? "Empirical T_G / T_N" :
    "Predicted (eq-rate-gap)"
end

spec = data(df_long) * mapping(
    :barρ2 => "Weighted ρ̄²",
    :ratio => "T_G / T_N",
    color = :quantity,
    marker = :μ0 => nonnumeric => "μ₀",
)

draw(
    visual(Scatter; markersize = 14) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

@cor-rate-gap connects directly to §Production solvers. glmnet's
`modified.Newton` mode and biglasso's `MM` mode both apply the gradient strategy
at the global $L_0 = 1/4$ to the intercept inside their IRLS inner solves; the
corollary predicts their pass counts should grow with $L_0/H_{00}$ at
$\mu_0 = 0.99$, matching the empirical ≈5× and ≈10× slowdowns reported in
@fig-real-glmnet and @fig-real-biglasso. skglm 0.5, the direct-CD solver,
exhibits the same scaling on a continuous trajectory in @fig-real-skglm: the
slow ramp from suboptimality $\sim 10^{-1}$ to $\sim 10^{-5}$ is the intercept
climb to $\mathrm{logit}(\mu_0)$ at step size $1/L_0$.

An obvious objection to @prp-gradient-partial is that adaptive step sizing
should rescue the gradient strategy: an Armijo line search ought to shrink
$\alpha$ until the iterate makes progress, irrespective of $L_0$. But starting
from the global-Lipschitz step $-\partial_0 F / L_0$ Armijo only *shrinks* the
step, and shrinking is the wrong direction when $H_{00} \ll L_0$: the step is
already too small, not too large. To recover the iterate-level curvature
$H_{00}$ a line search would need to *expand* the step beyond $1/L_0$, settling
near $1/H_{00}$. But the step of size $1/H_{00}$ applied to the gradient
direction is exactly the Newton step, so rescuing the gradient strategy
collapses it into Newton. @fig-mu-extreme confirms the shrinking-doesn't-help
direction empirically: a backtracking-Armijo variant of the gradient strategy
stalls identically to the bare-Lipschitz version, because the Lipschitz step
satisfies the sufficient-decrease condition on the first attempt and the line
search never fires.

The picture matches what production direct-CD solvers did at the time these
experiments were run. skglm 0.5 [@bertrand2022] used constant per-coordinate
Lipschitz steps and, on the unaveraged loss it works with internally, a step
$4/n$ on the intercept---exactly the gradient strategy as defined above (with
$L_0 = 1/4$ on the averaged loss), with no line search of any kind. The other
CD-based production packages we surveyed (glmnet, biglasso, LIBLINEAR, BlitzL1)
embed the intercept update inside an outer IRLS or proximal-Newton
linearization; we return to them in @sec-irls. None of the production CD solvers
we surveyed use a growth-allowing line search on the intercept alone.

#### A Safe Newton Variant

@prp-newton-coupling identifies the cold-start regime---large $|\partial_0 F|$
combined with rapidly varying $f''$---as the setting where an unguarded Newton
step on the intercept perturbs the next coefficient pass enough to matter. The
fix is to wrap the Newton direction $-\partial_0 F / H_{00}$ in an Armijo
backtracking line search: accept the full step ($\alpha = 1$) if it decreases
$F$ enough, otherwise halve $\alpha$ until it does. The Newton strategy as
implemented here folds this safeguard in directly, at a constant per-pass cost
in the easy regime and a logarithmic one when the linear model is inadequate;
the historical `DampedNewtonStrategy` is now a deprecated alias.

#### Constructed Failure Examples

We illustrate the predictions of the strategy comparison on synthetic
logistic-regression problems with $n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, and
$\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-extreme
#| fig-cap: As the response imbalance $\mu_0$ approaches one, the gradient
#|   strategy fails to reach the convergence tolerance within 1000 outer passes
#|   (@prp-gradient-partial prediction $H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$). A
#|   backtracking-Armijo variant of the gradient strategy stalls
#|   identically---the Lipschitz step satisfies sufficient decrease on the first
#|   attempt, so the line search never shrinks $\alpha$. The Newton and exact
#|   strategies are unaffected. Randomized cyclic CD.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-mu-extreme.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.μ0 = "μ₀ = " .* string.(df.μ0)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :μ0)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

The first prediction is @prp-gradient-partial: the gradient strategy's
correction is multiplied by $H_{00}/L_0$, which collapses as the response
imbalance $\mu_0$ approaches one. @fig-mu-extreme shows exactly this collapse:
the gradient strategy plateaus and fails to reach the tolerance within the
outer-pass budget at $\mu_0 = 0.99$, while the other strategies are essentially
unaffected.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-cold-start
#| fig-cap: With cyclic ordering and a cold-start intercept, the Newton
#|   strategy's per-coordinate Armijo guard absorbs the initial large
#|   $|\partial_0 F|$ transient that @prp-newton-coupling identifies as the
#|   unguarded-Newton failure mode; the Newton and exact trajectories agree
#|   across all $\mu_0$ levels.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-cold-start.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.μ0 = "μ₀ = " .* string.(df.μ0)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :μ0)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

The second prediction is @prp-newton-coupling: an unguarded Newton step on the
intercept can be perturbed by a large $|\partial_0 F|$ at cold start.
@fig-cold-start shows that the per-coordinate Armijo guard inside the Newton
strategy absorbs that transient: with cyclic ordering and the intercept
initialized at zero (so $|\partial_0 F|$ is large at pass one), the Newton
trajectory tracks the exact strategy across every $\mu_0$ level, including
$\mu_0 = 0.99$ where the unguarded analysis predicts the worst-case overshoot.
The exact strategy is competitive in this experiment but pays the
within-pass-drift cost identified in @prp-exact-cost.

#### Extension to Vector Intercepts

The scalar story extends almost verbatim to multinomial logistic regression with
$K$ classes, where the intercept is a vector $\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}$
under the reference-class parameterisation $\eta_{iK} = 0$. Writing
$\eta_{ik} = x_i^\intercal \beta_k + \beta_{0k}$ for $k = 1, \dots, K-1$ and
$p_{ik} = e^{\eta_{ik}}/\bigl(1 + \sum_{l<K} e^{\eta_{il}}\bigr)$, the
per-observation Hessian block has diagonal $p_{ik}(1 - p_{ik})$ and off-diagonal
$-p_{ik} p_{il}$. The intercept Hessian
$H_{00} = (1/n)\sum_i \bigl(\operatorname{diag}(p_{i,1:K-1}) - p_{i,1:K-1} p_{i,1:K-1}^\intercal\bigr)$
is a $(K-1) \times (K-1)$ matrix; the Newton strategy becomes a small block
solve $\delta = -H_{00}^{-1}\,\nabla_0 F$ followed by Armijo backtracking on the
loss along that direction. @thm-profile-equiv, @prp-exact-cost, and
@prp-newton-coupling all carry through with matrix-valued $H_{00}$ in place of
the scalar.

@prp-gradient-partial sharpens. The gradient strategy applies a uniform
Lipschitz bound $L_0$ across all classes, so the per-class fraction of the
correction is $H_{00,kk}/L_0 = \bigl((1/n)\sum_i p_{ik}(1 - p_{ik})\bigr)/L_0$.
With $K$ classes the diagonal $H_{00,kk}$ scales linearly with class prevalence,
so any rare class produces a microscopic intercept correction along that
coordinate while the dominant classes are well fit. Class imbalance is no longer
a corner case---with $K = 10$ and a uniform marginal, $\bar p_k = 0.1$ already,
and typical text or image-classification label distributions skew further. The
multinomial setting is where the imbalance failure of the gradient strategy is
the *common* regime rather than an extreme.

We implement block coordinate descent over classes: for each feature $j$ we
cycle through the $K-1$ class coefficients with element-wise $\ell_1$
soft-thresholding, and the intercept is updated as a vector once per pass. An
alternative is to cycle one class at a time with the others held fixed, as in
glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path; we return to that scheme below after the
block-CD findings.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-multinomial-imbalance
#| fig-cap: Imbalanced multinomial logistic ($K = 5$, marginal class
#|   probabilities $(0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.05, 0.05)$, $n = 500$, $p = 200$, $\lambda
#|   = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, three random seeds, cyclic CD). The gradient
#|   strategy stalls along the rare-class intercept components, exactly as
#|   predicted by the per-class fraction-of-correction $H_{00,kk}/L_0$. The
#|   Newton and exact strategies are visually indistinguishable.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-multinomial-imbalance.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.it = "seed = " .* string.(df.it)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :it)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative primal suboptimality", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

@fig-multinomial-imbalance reports relative primal suboptimality measured
against the lowest primal observed during each run; the multinomial CD solver
does not maintain a duality scaling.

The gradient strategy stalls, as expected. With the marginal class probabilities
above, the rare-class diagonal entries $H_{00,4,4}, H_{00,5,5}$ are roughly
twentieth-of-$L_0$ small, and the gradient strategy's per-class correction along
those coordinates is correspondingly microscopic. The strategy converges to the
same primal but takes roughly an order of magnitude longer.

The Newton and exact strategies collapse to a single visible curve. The
$(K-1)$-block Newton solve distributes each per-class correction through the
off-diagonal coupling $H_{00,kl} = -\sum_i p_{ik} p_{il}$, so the rare-class
step is computed in concert with the dominant-class step rather than amplified
proportionally to the rare-class gradient, and the Armijo guard absorbs any
residual cold-start transient that @prp-newton-coupling identifies in the scalar
setting. @fig-multinomial-sweep extends the test to a 2-D grid that shrinks the
rarest class probability $\bar p_K$ down to $0.005$ and grows the feature
amplitude to four times the anchor value. The Newton and exact trajectories
overlap in every one of the sixteen cells, while the gradient strategy stalls
monotonically harder as $\bar p_K$ shrinks and as amplitude grows. This is
consistent with a structural property of the $(K-1)$-block Hessian rather than a
tuning artefact of the single anchor configuration.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-multinomial-sweep
#| fig-cap: Multinomial logistic sweep over the rarest-class marginal $\bar p_K
#|   \in \{0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005\}$ (rows, top to bottom) and feature
#|   amplitude $\in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0\}$ (columns, left to right), on the
#|   same $K=5$, $n=500$, $p=200$, $s=5$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$,
#|   $\rho = 0.3$ design as @fig-multinomial-imbalance. Relative primal
#|   suboptimality versus outer-pass index, median over three seeds. The Newton
#|   and exact strategies overlap on a single curve in every cell; the gradient
#|   strategy stalls progressively harder as $\bar p_K$ shrinks (down the rows)
#|   and as amplitude grows (across the columns). The anchor cell (top-left)
#|   reproduces the trajectories of @fig-multinomial-imbalance.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-multinomial-imbalance-sweep.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals, :pass])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

agg = combine(
    groupby(df, [:p_K, :amplitude, :strategy, :pass]),
    :relgaps => median => :relgaps,
)

agg.p_K_str = "p̄_K = " .* string.(agg.p_K)
agg.amp_str = "amp = " .* string.(agg.amplitude)

spec = data(agg) * mapping(
    :pass => "Pass",
    :relgaps => "Relative primal suboptimality",
    color = :strategy,
    row = :p_K_str => sorter("p̄_K = 0.05", "p̄_K = 0.02", "p̄_K = 0.01", "p̄_K = 0.005"),
    col = :amp_str => sorter("amp = 0.5", "amp = 1.0", "amp = 1.5", "amp = 2.0"),
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 600)),
)
```

Practically, this simplifies the recommendation in the multinomial setting: use
the bare Newton block step. The damping safeguard that mattered for the scalar
cold-start is already built in.

The same pattern holds on real high-dimensional multinomial data. The Yeoh2002
pediatric ALL gene-expression panel\ [@yeoh2002] is a $K = 6$ subtype problem on
$n = 248$ samples and $p = 12\,625$ genes with class marginals BCR\ $=
6\%$, MLL\ $= 8\%$, E2A\ $= 11\%$, T\ $= 17\%$, Hyperdip\ $= 26\%$, and TEL\ $=
32\%$. The two rare classes BCR and MLL sit in exactly the regime where the
per-class fraction $H_{00,kk}/L_0$ predicts a stall under the gradient strategy.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-multinomial
#| fig-cap: Multinomial logistic on Yeoh2002 ($n = 248$, $p = 12\,625$, $K = 6$
#|   pediatric ALL subtypes; rare classes BCR at 6\% and MLL at 8\%) at $\lambda
#|   = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$ under cyclic CD. The gradient strategy needs $422$
#|   outer passes to reach relative primal suboptimality $10^{-6}$ where the
#|   Newton-class strategies need $142$, a $\approx 3\times$ ratio driven by the
#|   two rare classes. The Newton and exact trajectories coincide exactly---the
#|   same block-Hessian collapse seen in @fig-multinomial-imbalance. Relative
#|   primal suboptimality measured against the lowest primal observed during
#|   each run, since the multinomial CD solver does not maintain a duality
#|   scaling.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "real-multinomial-yeoh.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative primal suboptimality",
    color = :strategy,
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300))
)
```

@fig-real-multinomial reproduces the synthetic pattern on a genuine $p > n$
gene-expression multinomial problem with rare classes: the gradient strategy
stalls along the rare-class intercept components while the Newton-class
strategies---including exact---collapse onto a single curve. The slowdown ratio
($\approx 3\times$ at relative suboptimality $10^{-6}$) is milder than the
$\approx 15\times$ ratio of @fig-multinomial-imbalance because Yeoh2002's rarest
class is at $6\,\%$ rather than the $5\,\%$ floor of the synthetic design, and
the penalty contribution at $n \ll p$ damps the absolute scale of the per-pass
intercept correction. The qualitative diagnostic is intact: rare classes are the
regime where the gradient strategy fails the multinomial intercept update on
real data, exactly as the block-Schur analysis predicts.

The class-by-class scheme of glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path tells a
different but parallel story. Holding all $\eta_{il}$ for $l \neq k$ fixed, the
marginal subproblem in class $k$'s linear predictors $\eta_{ik}$ is, up to a
per-observation offset $\log\bigl(1 + \sum_{l \neq k} e^{\eta_{il}}\bigr)$, a
scalar logistic regression. The scalar theory of @prp-gradient-partial therefore
applies *per class*, and any rare class with extreme per-class response
imbalance triggers exactly the gradient-strategy failure documented in the
binary setting---now along the rare class's intercept coordinate specifically.
The multinomial setting hits the gradient-strategy failure mode through two
independent mechanisms then: rare-class diagonal scaling under block CD, and
rare-class scalar imbalance under class-by-class CD. The Newton-strategy
recommendation transfers to both schemes.

### Connection to IRLS {#sec-irls}

The analysis so far targets *direct* coordinate descent on $F$, in which the
weights $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$ are recomputed after every coefficient
update. A widely used alternative---and the one taken by glmnet
[@friedman2010]---is iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)
[@mccullagh1989]: at the current iterate $(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)})$,
form a weighted least squares majorizer
$$
\tilde F^{(t)}(\beta_0, \beta)
  \;=\;
  \frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^{(t)}
    \bigl( z_i^{(t)} - \beta_0 - x_i^\intercal \beta \bigr)^2,
$$
with working response $z_i^{(t)} = \eta_i^{(t)} - r_i^{(t)} / w_i^{(t)}$,
run inner CD on $\tilde F^{(t)}$, then re-linearize. Two weight choices are
used in practice: *local* weights $w_i^{(t)} = f''(\eta_i^{(t)}; y_i)$
(glmnet's `type.logistic = "Newton"`), and *MM-majorized* weights replacing
$w_i^{(t)}$ by a global upper bound on $f''$ (e.g. $w_i \equiv 1/4$ for
logistic; glmnet's `type.logistic = "modified.Newton"`, following the MM
tradition of @hunter2004).

Inside one inner solve with local weights, $\tilde F^{(t)}$ is quadratic in
$\beta_0$ with curvature $(1/n)\sum_i w_i^{(t)} = H_{00}$, so the inner
Lipschitz constant satisfies $L_0^{\text{inner}} = H_{00}$. The fraction
$H_{00} / L_0^{\text{inner}} = 1$ in @prp-gradient-partial, and Newton on a
quadratic is exact, so the gradient, Newton, and exact strategies all coincide
on the inner subproblem. The strategy distinction this paper analyzes is
therefore specific to direct-CD solvers (e.g. skglm) and does not arise within
one local-weight IRLS inner solve.

The MM-majorized variant tells a different story. Replacing $w_i^{(t)}$ by the
constant majorant $1/4$ in the logistic case, the closed-form inner intercept
update on $\tilde F^{(t)}$ is
$$
\beta_0 \;\gets\; \beta_0 + \frac{4}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - p_i)
  \;=\; \beta_0 - \frac{1}{L_0}\, \partial_0 F,
\qquad L_0 = 1/4,
$$
which is exactly the gradient strategy of this paper, taken with the global
Lipschitz step. @prp-gradient-partial therefore applies directly to glmnet's
`modified.Newton` mode: under response imbalance, the per-iteration correction
fraction $H_{00} / L_0$ shrinks and the intercept update slows in proportion,
approaching a true stall only in the limit $\mu_0 \to 1$. There is a historical
irony here---MM majorization was introduced for numerical stability of the
working response $z_i$ when $w_i \to 0$, which is the same imbalance regime
where the resulting update converges slowly. For Poisson loss no global upper
bound on $f''$ exists, so the MM construction is not directly available; glmnet
uses local-weight IRLS for Poisson, where the collapse of the previous paragraph
applies instead.

Across IRLS linearizations the weights $w_i^{(t)}$ change with $\eta^{(t)}$, so
even a fully resolved inner intercept becomes stale once the weights are
recomputed. This outer-level drift is analogous to but distinct from the
within-pass drift of @prp-exact-cost, which is direct-CD-specific.

The practical map is therefore richer than the direct-CD analysis alone
suggests. @tbl-classification summarises where each production solver falls.
Among the CD-based packages we surveyed, only skglm 0.5 and earlier are genuine
direct-CD-gradient-strategy realizations on the original loss. The remaining
solvers---glmnet, biglasso, adelie, LIBLINEAR, BlitzL1, Lasso.jl, ncvreg---all
linearize before doing CD, either via IRLS or via proximal-Newton on a quadratic
upper bound. Within those families the within-package mode toggles are what
isolate the strategy comparison: glmnet's `Newton` vs `modified.Newton` and
biglasso's `Newton` vs `MM` toggle precisely the weight scheme of
@prp-gradient-partial. (Scikit-learn's L1-logistic path either delegates to
LIBLINEAR or uses SAGA, the latter a variance-reduced stochastic-gradient method
that falls outside the CD framework analyzed here. celer's L1-logistic estimator
does not support an intercept at all in version 0.7.4, and its documentation
redirects users with logistic needs to skglm; it is therefore absent from the
table.)

  | Solver                                        | Family                | Intercept Update on the Original Loss                       |
  | :-------------------------------------------- | :-------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------- |
  | skglm 0.5                                     | Constant-Lipschitz CD | Gradient ($L_0 = 1/4$)                                      |
  | glmnet (`type.logistic = "modified.Newton"`)  | MM-IRLS               | Gradient ($L_0 = 1/4$) per outer iteration                  |
  | biglasso (`alg.logistic = "MM"`)              | MM-IRLS               | Gradient ($L_0 = 1/4$) per outer iteration                  |
  | glmnet (`type.logistic = "Newton"`)           | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | biglasso (`alg.logistic = "Newton"`, default) | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | Lasso.jl                                      | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | ncvreg                                        | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | adelie                                        | Local-IRLS            | Implicit, via weighted-centered-features parameterization   |
  | LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET, L1-LR)                  | Prox-Newton           | Convergence on the quadratic; intercept unregularized       |
  | BlitzL1                                       | Prox-Newton           | Combined-direction backtrack + post-step Newton convergence |

  : Classification of CD-based production solvers by algorithmic family and by
    the intercept update they realize on the original loss. Local-IRLS and
    prox-Newton solvers freeze the Hessian at the start of a subproblem, so the
    three strategies of this paper coincide *within* one subproblem; the
    distinction reappears only when comparing weight schemes across outer
    iterations (rows three to six). BlitzL1 additionally follows each
    prox-Newton subproblem with a separate sequence of 1-D Newton iterations on
    the intercept on the original loss; LIBLINEAR arrives at the same end
    without that loop, because its inner CD already drives the unregularized
    intercept to its conditional minimum on the quadratic. {#tbl-classification}

A consequence of the table is that two production solvers---LIBLINEAR
(newGLMNET) and BlitzL1---end up with the exact strategy on the intercept at the
boundary of each prox-Newton step. BlitzL1 arrives there by design, with an
explicit 1-D Newton convergence loop on the original loss after each subproblem;
LIBLINEAR arrives there as a byproduct of leaving the intercept unregularized
inside the inner CD, whose QP convergence carries the intercept to its
conditional minimum on the quadratic. The analysis in @prp-exact-cost penalises
exact-strategy within direct CD because the inner Hessian drifts between
iterations; that critique does not apply at the prox-Newton boundary, where the
next subproblem's Hessian is recomputed anyway. The structural distinction
between the families thus carries over to a sensible recommendation: use Newton
on the intercept within direct CD, and run the exact strategy at the
linearization boundary inside IRLS or prox-Newton. The production solvers that
fit serious imbalanced-GLM problems in practice appear to have arrived at
exactly this prescription.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-irls-comparison
#| fig-cap: Imbalanced logistic ($\mu_0 = 0.99$, $n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s =
#|   10$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, three random seeds). MM-IRLS tracks
#|   Direct-CD with the gradient strategy as the algebra above predicts---both
#|   stall at the same per-iteration correction fraction. Local-weight IRLS
#|   converges, matching the strategy collapse argument. The Local-IRLS curve
#|   uses Newton at the inner level; the gradient and exact strategies coincide
#|   with it numerically (verified in unit tests).

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-irls-comparison.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.it = "seed = " .* string.(df.it)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :it)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

@fig-irls-comparison realizes both predictions empirically: MM-IRLS stalls on
the same plateau as Direct-CD with the gradient strategy under $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
while Local-IRLS converges on the same problem. The strategy-collapse claim
within Local-IRLS is verified numerically in the unit tests rather than the
figure, since by construction the three strategies produce identical iterates on
the inner quadratic.

A reader may notice that Local-IRLS also outpaces Direct-CD with the Newton
strategy on this problem. This reflects the broader trade-off between
algorithmic families rather than a comparison of intercept strategies: IRLS-CD
enjoys a constant inner Hessian and locally quadratic outer convergence, which
favours it on canonical-link GLMs where the linearization is tight. Direct-CD
has the edge when $f'''$ is large (e.g.\
Poisson with extreme rates, where each linearization is loose far from the
current iterate), when working-response instability under saturation matters, or
when screening and working-set methods (standard in modern $\ell_1$ solvers)
compose poorly with re-linearization [@bertrand2022]. Our strategy analysis is
orthogonal to this family choice: within either family, the recommendation
against the gradient strategy and in favour of Newton carries through.

### Geometric Illustration

```{julia}
#| label: fig-parametric
#| fig-cap: Example illustrating the three main intercept fitting strategies
#|   considered in our paper on a simple problem with one feature and an
#|   intercept.
#| fig-show: true
#| message: false

using Intercepts

n = 100
p = 1
k = 10
μ0 = 0.9

X, y = generatedata(
    n, p; response = :binomial, μ0 = μ0, x_type = :normal, x_density = 0.9, ρ = 0.99, s = k, amplitude = 1,
)

strategies = [
    (strategy = GradientStrategy(), name = "Gradient"),
    (strategy = NewtonStrategy(), name = "Newton"),
    (strategy = ExactStrategy(), name = "Exact"),
]

reg = 0.2

results = [
    cdsolver(
            X,
            y,
            reg,
            lossfun = LogisticLoss(),
            intercept_strategy = s.strategy,
            save_history = true,
        ) for s in strategies
]

λ = results[1].λ

β0 = range(-0.5, 3.5, length = 100)
β = range(-0.5, 1.2, length = 100)
grid = [(b0, b) for b0 in β0, b in β]

primal_values = zeros(size(grid))

for (i, (b0, b)) in enumerate(grid)
    η = b0 .+ X[:, 1] * b
    primal_values[i] = loss(LogisticLoss(), η, y) + λ * abs(b)
end

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xlabel = "Intercept (β₀)",
    ylabel = "Coefficient (β₁)",
)

levels = geomspace(minimum(primal_values), maximum(primal_values), 20)

contour!(β0, β, primal_values, levels = levels, colormap = :grays)

for (res, s) in zip(results, strategies)
    scatterlines!(res.intercepts, dropdims(res.coefs, dims = 1), label = s.name)
end

fig[1, 2] = Legend(fig, ax)

fig
```

## Results

### Methodology and Reproducibility {#sec-methodology}

All internal-solver experiments use the `Intercepts` Julia package on Julia
1.11+ with the default OpenBLAS. We report outer-pass counts as the primary work
metric: one pass is one sweep through all $p$ coordinates plus an intercept
update, and "passes to tolerance" use a target relative duality gap of $10^{-8}$
unless noted. Pass budgets (`maxit`) are set generously (1000 for the
single-$\lambda$ figures, 5000 for the heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg) and are
clipped only at the figure level when the gradient strategy fails to reach the
tolerance; those points appear at the budget cap. All synthetic designs are
standardized (zero mean, unit variance per column) and use cyclic coordinate
ordering unless we explicitly compare orderings; the AR(1) feature correlation
parameter is $\rho = 0.6$ by default. Random seeds are fixed per experiment
script. The heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg replicates each cell across three
seeds; the other figures use a single seed because cell-to-cell variability is
dwarfed by the strategy effect we are isolating.

Real-data experiments load LIBSVM problems via `LIBSVMdata.jl` 0.1.4 and the
solver standardizes each column internally before fitting. The production-solver
panel runs glmnet 4.1-10 (R), biglasso 1.6-1 (R), adelie 1.0-8 (R), skglm 0.5
(Python), LIBLINEAR through scikit-learn's `solver="liblinear"` wrapper, and
BlitzL1 at commit `aef8d02` on the shared standardized problem produced by
`experiments/sim-real-problem.jl`. The shared problem is regenerated from
`Random.seed!(2025)`; the production drivers are otherwise deterministic given
the cached `X.csv` / `y.csv`, so each driver runs once per tolerance setting
with no per-driver seed or per-cell replication. Each driver sweeps its native
tolerance knob and writes a CSV under `results/real-solvers/`, which the figures
in @sec-production-solvers read directly. The sweeps cover: glmnet `thresh` and
biglasso `eps` from $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-13}$ in half-decade steps; skglm `tol`
over the same span in quarter-decade steps; LIBLINEAR `tol` from $10^{-1}$ to
$10^{-8}$ and BlitzL1 `tol` from $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-10}$, both in half-decade
steps; adelie's coupled `tol`/`irls_tol` only down to $10^{-3.5}$ because the
outer IRLS convergence criterion exhausts progress long before any iterate cap
at tighter settings. Per-driver iterate caps (glmnet/biglasso `max.iter`
$= 10^{6}$, adelie `irls_max_iters` $= 10^{6}$, skglm `max_iter` $= 5000$,
LIBLINEAR `max_iter` $= 5000$, BlitzL1 `max_iter` $= 500$) are set generously;
operating points that hit the cap appear at the cap.

All experiment outputs are cached. Internal-solver scripts at
`experiments/sim-*.jl` write `.jld2` files to `results/`; production-solver
scripts write `.csv` to `results/real-solvers/`. The paper re-renders from
cache, so to refresh a cell re-run the corresponding script. The Julia, R, and
Python toolchains are pinned by `devenv.nix` (the `glmnet`, `biglasso`,
`adelie`, `skglm`, and `blitzl1` versions above included) and all use their
default OpenBLAS builds with no thread pinning. Hardware: a single x86_64 Linux
workstation; wall-clock numbers in this paper are indicative rather than
benchmark-grade. Source code and cached results ship with the paper repository.

### Simulated Data

The first prediction we test in §Theory is @prp-gradient-partial: the gradient
strategy's effective per-pass step on the intercept is the bare gradient step
shrunk by $H_{00}/L_0$, so the strategy slows as the imbalance $\mu_0$ pushes
